title: Drones Drop Food to a City Running Out of It
summary:
What if the grocery stores in your town all closed, and the nearest food was 20 kilometres away? That is what life is like right now in Oleshky, a city in Ukraine.

Oleshky sits just three kilometres south of the Dnipro River. That river is the front line between Ukrainian forces on one side and Russian forces on the other. Before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, about 20,000 people lived there. Now Ukrainian officials think only about 6,000 remain, including roughly 200 children.

On Saturday, Ukrainian officials say they flew drones over the city and dropped four tonnes of food — boxes of food and cooking oil — at 100 different locations. It was done in waves, using several military units. Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, a regional official, said the aid "will give people the opportunity to live there for up to a month." But he warned that Russian troops seized supplies from civilians in some cases.

Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, told the United Nations that Russia has put the city under a "full blockade" and is blocking humanitarian aid. Russia says the city does have serious shortages and that its forces are working to fix the problems.

One woman told CBC News her 70-year-old mother-in-law walked six hours to leave Oleshky. She said people there have been trading vegetables for eggs and searching for food — sometimes finding only two potatoes and two pieces of garlic.
why_it_matters: When shops close and roads are not safe, getting dinner can depend on strangers far away deciding to help — which is why people argue about who is allowed to deliver food in a war.

background_read: Ukraine (a country in Eastern Europe) has been fighting a war since Russia launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022; the Dnipro River is part of the front line, where the two armies face each other.

The United Nations (a group where almost all countries meet to talk about big world problems) hears complaints like this one — and international law says that in a war, ordinary people must be allowed to get food and medicine.
CBC News (a news company from Canada) spoke to a family whose 70-year-old relative walked six hours to get out of the city.
Article_Structure: WHO: About 6,000 people still living in Oleshky, including roughly 200 children, plus Ukraine's drone units, regional official Oleksandr Tolokonnikov and Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha.
WHAT: Ukrainian drones dropped four tonnes of food — boxes of food and cooking oil — at 100 different locations, flying in waves using several military units.
WHERE: Oleshky, a city in Ukraine just three kilometres south of the Dnipro River, which is the front line between Ukrainian and Russian forces.
WHY: The city is running out of food after years of war and what Ukraine calls a 'full blockade'; officials say the airdrop will let people live there for up to a month.
